Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesDavid seeks God upon former experience.1–4He vows to serve God.5–8
Seeking shelter on the higher Rock (verses 1–4)

David began with tears and prayer, but ended with praise. A soul lifted toward God may recover peace and a sense of its true condition.

Wherever we find ourselves, there is a way open to the throne of grace. When earthly comforts are withdrawn, their absence should turn us toward God, the fountain of every comfort.

An overwhelmed heart may still be lifted up in prayer. Indeed, the act of crying to God can sustain and relieve it. Weeping should make us more earnest in prayer, not prevent prayer.

God's power and promises are a rock higher than we can reach by ourselves. That Rock is Christ.

David was like a shipwrecked sailor tossed by waves at the foot of a rock so high that he could not climb it without help. Though he wanted to rest upon divine mercy, he knew he could not place himself securely on the Rock of salvation.

We therefore need God to lead us to Christ and establish us in him. In him there is safety; in ourselves there is none.

David resolved to make service to God his constant occupation. Everyone who expects the Lord to be a shelter and strong tower must do the same. God's grace will then be a continual source of comfort.

Service grounded in everlasting promises (verses 5–8)

God has a people who fear his name, and a particular inheritance belongs to them. Even now they experience comfort in the soul, an advance pledge of happiness to come.

Those who fear God have enough in him and should not complain. We need desire no better inheritance than theirs.

Those who live before God, serve him and walk in reverent fear live to a good purpose in this world; they will dwell before him forever.

Henry also understands these words to refer especially to the Messiah, of whom the angel said that he would receive David's throne and reign without end (Luke 1:32).

The promises of God do not make prayer unnecessary. They encourage and strengthen prayer.

No protection is better than God's mercy and truth. Through the grace and truth that came by Jesus Christ, believers have reason to praise him whatever their outward circumstances.

A renewed experience of God's mercy and truth toward his people in Christ is therefore the chief reason for our joy and thanksgiving.
classic_reading:
[Ps.61.1-Ps.61.4]
Chapter 61
Chapter Outline
David seeks God upon former experience. | (1-4) |
He vows to serve God. | (5-8) |
Verses 1-4
David begins with prayers and tears, but ends with praise. Thus the soul, being lifted up to God, returns to the enjoyment of itself. Wherever we are, we have liberty to draw near to God, and may find a way open to the throne of grace. And that which separates us from other comforts, should drive us nearer to God, the fountain of all comfort. Though the heart is overwhelmed, yet it may be lifted up to God in prayer. Nay, I will cry unto thee, for by that means it will be supported and relieved. Weeping must quicken praying, and not deaden it. God's power and promise are a rock that is higher than we are. This rock is Christ. On the Divine mercy, as on a rock, David desired to rest his soul; but he was like a ship-wrecked sailor, exposed to the billows at the bottom of a rock too high for him to climb without help. David found that he could not be fixed on the Rock of salvation, unless the Lord placed him upon it. As there is safety in Him, and none in ourselves, let us pray to be led to and fixed upon Christ our Rock. The service of God shall be his constant work and business: all must make it so who expect to find God their shelter and strong tower. The grace of God shall be his constant comfort.
[Ps.61.5-Ps.61.8]
Verses 5-8
There is a people in the world that fear God's name. There is a heritage peculiar to that people; present comforts in the soul, earnests of future bliss. Those that fear God have enough in him, and must not complain. We need desire no better heritage than that of those who fear God. Those abide to good purpose in this world, who abide before God, serve him, and walk in his fear; those who do so, shall abide before him for ever. And these words are to be applied to Him of whom the angel said, the Lord shall give unto him the throne of his father David, and of his kingdom there shall be no end, [Luke.1.32] Lu 1:32. God's promises, and our faith in them, are not to do away, but to encourage prayer. We need not desire to be better secured than under the protection of God's mercy and truth. And if we partake of that grace and truth which came by Jesus Christ, we may praise him, whatever be our outward circumstances. But renewed experience of God's mercy and truth towards his people in Christ, is the main matter of our joy in him, and our praise unto him.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesDavid's confidence in God.1–7No trust to be put in worldly things.8–12
David waits quietly on God (verses 1–7)

We find both duty and comfort when our souls wait upon the Lord: cheerfully placing ourselves and all our concerns under his will and wisdom, accepting the ways of his Providence and patiently trusting his goodness for the outcome.

David had good reasons for such confidence. God's grace had sustained him, and divine Providence had delivered him.

God alone could be his Rock and salvation. Created beings have no strength independently of him, so David looked beyond them to the Lord himself.

Trust in God establishes the heart. When God is for us, we need not fear what other human beings may do.

Remembering former occasions when waiting upon the Lord proved good, we should continually encourage our souls to depend upon him. This produces greater inner quietness.

If God saves my soul, I may safely leave everything else to his judgment, knowing that he will direct it toward my salvation.

As David's faith became steadier, his joy rose toward holy triumph. Meditation and prayer are blessed means of strengthening both faith and hope.

Trust God, not people or wealth (verses 8–12)

Those who have discovered comfort in God's ways naturally invite others to join them. We lose nothing when others share these blessings.

Trust him at all times—not reserving for ourselves or any created thing the confidence that belongs to him alone.

Look to him for guidance in doubt, protection in danger, provision in need and strength for every good word and work.

Pouring out the heart means placing our needs and desires before God, then patiently submitting those desires to his will.

God is a refuge for all who come to take shelter in him.

Do not make people the foundation of your hope. An ordinary crowd is as changeable as the wind; great and wealthy people may promise much, but those depending upon their promises are often disappointed.

Weighed in Scripture's balance, all human ability to make us happy is lighter than vanity.

Even wealth gained honestly can become dangerous when our affections rest upon it. A pleasant and prosperous world can turn our hearts away from God.

A consistent believer receives possessions as a trust from God, managing them for his glory like a steward who will give an account.

God has declared that power belongs to him. He can judge and destroy. Mercy also belongs to him.

The fact that he rewards his people's imperfect service and forgives their transgressions for the Redeemer's sake displays his abundant mercy.

Let us therefore abound in his work and expect every blessing from his grace alone.
classic_reading:
[Ps.62.1-Ps.62.7]
Chapter 62
Chapter Outline
David's confidence in God. | (1-7) |
No trust to be put in worldly things. | (8-12) |
Verses 1-7
We are in the way both of duty and comfort, when our souls wait upon God; when we cheerfully give up ourselves, and all our affairs, to his will and wisdom; when we leave ourselves to all the ways of his providence, and patiently expect the event, with full satisfaction in his goodness. See the ground and reason of this dependence. By his grace he has supported me, and by his providence delivered me. He only can be my Rock and my salvation; creatures are nothing without him, therefore I will look above them to him. Trusting in God, the heart is fixed. If God be for us, we need not fear what man can do against us. David having put his confidence in God, foresees the overthrow of his enemies. We have found it good to wait upon the Lord, and should charge our souls to have such constant dependence upon him, as may make us always easy. If God will save my soul, I may well leave every thing else to his disposal, knowing all shall turn to my salvation. And as David's faith in God advances to an unshaken stedfastness, so his joy in God improves into a holy triumph. Meditation and prayer are blessed means of strengthening faith and hope.
[Ps.62.8-Ps.62.12]
Verses 8-12
Those who have found the comfort of the ways of God themselves, will invite others into those ways; we shall never have the less for others sharing with us. the good counsel given is, to trust wholly in God. We must so trust in him at all times, as not at any time to put that trust in ourselves, or in any creature, which is to be put in him only. Trust in him to guide us when in doubt, to protect us when in danger, to supply us when in want, to strengthen us for every good word and work. We must lay out wants and our wishes before him, and then patiently submit our wills to his: this is pouring out our hearts. God is a refuge for all, even for as many as will take shelter in him. The psalmist warns against trusting in men. The multitude, those of low degree, are changeable as the wind. The rich and noble seem to have much in their power, and lavish promises; but those that depend on them, are disappointed. Weighed in the balance of Scripture, all that man can do to make us happy is lighter than vanity itself. It is hard to have riches, and not to trust in them if they increase, though by lawful and honest means; but we must take heed, lest we set our affections unduly upon them. A smiling world is the most likely to draw the heart from God, on whom alone it should be set. The consistent believer receives all from God as a trust; and he seeks to use it to his glory, as a steward who must render an account. God hath spoken as it were once for all, that power belongs to him alone. He can punish and destroy. Mercy also belongs to him; and his recompensing the imperfect services of those that believe in him, blotting out their transgressions for the Redeemer's sake, is a proof of abundant mercy, and encourages us to trust in him. Let us trust in his mercy and grace, and abound in his work, expecting mercies from him alone.

David thirsts for God (verses 1 and 2)

“Early will I seek you.”

A true Christian devotes the morning to God. As the eyes of the body open, the eyes of understanding should awaken to righteousness.

Such a believer wakes with a thirst for comfort the world cannot provide, and immediately turns in prayer to the Fountain of the water of life.

The immortal soul cannot be satisfied by anything this sinful world offers. It seeks happiness in God as its portion.

The more actively faith and hope work, the more the world resembles a dry and weary desert.

Then the heart longs for the joys of heaven, of which believers receive some foretastes through God's appointed ordinances here on earth.

God's love is better than life (verses 3–6)

Even during affliction there are reasons to praise God.

A believer rightly values God's loving-kindness above earthly life. That kindness gives spiritual life, which is better than bodily existence.

Our praise should therefore arise from holy joy. Lips offering praise should be joyful lips.

David was continually in danger. Anxiety and fear kept him awake through exhausting nights.

Yet he found consolation in remembering God.

When the Lord's mercies come to mind during the night watches, they sustain the soul and make even the darkness cheerful.

How happy will be the final morning, when believers awaken satisfied with God's likeness and enjoy his fullness!

There will be no night, grief or sighing there, only joyful praise.

Following God because his hand upholds us (verses 7–11)

Christians may sometimes speak with the confidence David expresses here, though too often their souls cling to the dust.

Having entrusted ourselves to the Lord, we ought to rest in his care without surrendering to fear.

Those who earnestly follow God would soon fail if his right hand did not uphold them.

He is the One who strengthens and comforts.

The psalmist expected that, although he was sowing in tears, he would eventually reap in joy.

The Messiah, our Prince, rejoices in God. He has entered the joy set before him, and his glory will be complete at his second coming.

Blessed Lord, let our desire for you increase every hour. May our love remain fixed upon you, and may all our joy and satisfaction be found in you.

Be everything to us during our present wilderness journey and bring us home to enjoy you forever.
classic_reading:
[Ps.63.1-Ps.63.2]
Chapter 63
Chapter Outline
David's desire toward God. | (1-2) |
His satisfaction in God. | (3-6) |
His dependence upon God, and assurance of safety. | (7-11) |
Verses 1-2
Early will I seek thee. The true Christian devotes to God the morning hour. He opens the eyes of his understanding with those of his body, and awakes each morning to righteousness. He arises with a thirst after those comforts which the world cannot give, and has immediate recourse by prayer to the Fountain of the water of life. The true believer is convinced, that nothing in this sinful world can satisfy the wants and desires of his immortal soul; he expects his happiness from God, as his portion. When faith and hope are most in exercise, the world appears a weary desert, and the believer longs for the joys of heaven, of which he has some foretastes in the ordinances of God upon earth.
[Ps.63.3-Ps.63.6]
Verses 3-6
Even in affliction we need not want matter for praise. When this is the regular frame of a believer's mind, he values the loving-kindness of God more than life. God's loving-kindness is our spiritual life, and that is better than temporal life. We must praise God with joyful lips; we must address ourselves to the duties of religion with cheerfulness, and speak forth the praises of God from a principle of holy joy. Praising lips must be joyful lips. David was in continual danger; care and fear held his eyes waking, and gave him wearisome nights; but he comforted himself with thoughts of God. The mercies of God, when called to mind in the night watches, support the soul, making darkness cheerful. How happy will be that last morning, when the believer, awaking up after the Divine likeness, shall be satisfied with all the fulness of God, and praise him with joyful lips, where there is no night, and where sorrow and sighing flee away!
[Ps.63.7-Ps.63.11]
Verses 7-11
True Christians can, in some measure, and at some times, make use of the strong language of David, but too commonly our souls cleave to the dust. Having committed ourselves to God, we must be easy and pleased, and quiet from the fear of evil. Those that follow hard after God, would soon fail, if God's right hand did not uphold them. It is he that strengthens us and comforts us. The psalmist doubts not but that though now sowing in tears, he should reap in joy. Messiah the Prince shall rejoice in God; he is already entered into the joy set before him, and his glory will be completed at his second coming. Blessed Lord, let our desire towards thee increase every hour; let our love be always upon thee; let all our enjoyment be in thee, and all our satisfaction from thee. Be thou all in all to us while we remain in the present wilderness state, and bring us home to the everlasting enjoyment of thee for ever.

Prayer against dangerous speech and plots (verses 1–6)

The psalmist earnestly asked God to preserve him from paralyzing fear.

The tongue is a small part of the body, but it boasts of great things and can do terrible harm.

Upright people become targets of the wicked, who refuse to speak peacefully either about them or to them.

No human precaution can fully guard against a false tongue.

Doing wrong is evil, but encouraging oneself and others to do wrong is even worse.

A heart firmly committed to wrongdoing shows how deeply it has hardened.

At the root of all wickedness lies a practical denial of God's complete knowledge.

The greatest comfort of a good cause and a clear conscience often appears when no person can rescue us from our enemies and God alone remains our help.

He is always present to save.

The Lord judges evil and vindicates the innocent (verses 7–10)

When God turns upon wrongdoers the mischief they planned for others, their own schemes become a dreadful judgment against them.

Those who delight in cursing will find that curses return upon them.

Observers should recognize God's hand in these events; otherwise they fail to learn from the workings of Providence.

The righteous rejoice in the Lord, not because fellow human beings suffer or perish, but because God is glorified, his word fulfilled and innocence effectively defended.

They do not base their joy on people, their own cleverness, strength, riches, morality or any created pleasure.

They rejoice in Christ, in whom God's true people are justified and may glory, and in everything he has done and continues to be for them.
classic_reading:
[Ps.64.1-Ps.64.6]
Chapter 64
Chapter Outline
Prayer for deliverance. | (1-6) |
The destruction of the wicked, encouragement to the righteous. | (7-10) |
Verses 1-6
The psalmist earnestly begs of God to preserve him from disquieting fear. The tongue is a little member, but it boasts great things. The upright man is the mark at which the wicked aim, they cannot speak peaceably either of him or to him. There is no guard against a false tongue. It is bad to do wrong, but worse to encourage ourselves and one another in it. It is a sign that the heart is hardened to the greatest degree, when it is thus fully set to do evil. A practical disbelief of God's knowledge of all things, is at the bottom of every wickedness. The benefit of a good cause and a good conscience, appears most when nothing can help a man against his enemies, save God alone, who is always a present help.
[Ps.64.7-Ps.64.10]
Verses 7-10
When God brings upon men the mischiefs they have desired on others, it is weight enough to sink a man to the lowest hell. Those who love cursing, it shall come upon them. Those who behold this shall understand, and observe God's hand in all; unless we do so, we are not likely to profit by the dispensations of Providence. The righteous shall be glad in the Lord; not glad of the misery and ruin of their fellow-creatures, but glad that God is glorified, and his word fulfilled, and the cause of injured innocence pleaded effectually. They rejoice not in men, nor in themselves, nor in any creature, or creature enjoyments, nor in their wisdom, strength, riches, or righteousness; but in Christ, in whom all the seed of Israel are justified and glory, and in what he is to them, and has done for them.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesGod is to be praised in the kingdom of grace.1–5In the kingdom of providence.6–13
Praise in the kingdom of grace (verses 1–5)

All praise offered to God from earth comes from Zion, arising through the Spirit of Christ and becoming acceptable through him.

At times praise is silent because no words can express the greatness of God's goodness.

The Lord reveals himself at a mercy seat, ready to hear everyone who comes by faith in Jesus Christ.

Our sins prevail against us.

We cannot balance them with any personal righteousness.

Yet by God's free mercy, and through a righteousness he himself supplies, our transgressions will not bring us into condemnation.

Communion with God is a great blessing. It means enjoying fellowship with him as One we love and value, making devotion to him the ordinary business of our lives.

Such fellowship is possible only because God freely chooses to welcome us.

His house contains abundance enough to satisfy every soul—enough for everyone and enough for each, always ready and without money or price.

Wherever we live, faith and prayer allow us to maintain this fellowship and receive comfort.

But sinners receive these blessings only through Jesus Christ, who approaches the Father as our Advocate and Surety.

Praise in the kingdom of Providence (verses 6–13)

The almighty strength that establishes mountains also supports the believer.

The word that calms stormy seas can silence the enemies of God's people.

Morning and evening bring different blessings: the watchman longs for morning, while the laborer welcomes evening's shade.

Some understand the psalm's language as a reference to morning and evening sacrifices.

Whatever the interpretation, let daily worship—both private and with our families—be a necessary duty and a cherished comfort.

The fruitful earth depends upon gifts from above, and every good and perfect gift comes from God.

He generously enriches a world full of human sin. Surely he has both power and willingness to feed the souls of his people.

These earthly provisions picture greater spiritual blessings.

Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, rises upon sinners, and the Holy Spirit, the river of God full of living water, brings salvation and life.

By that work, barren hearts become fruitful in good deeds, and whole nations are transformed more wonderfully than the ground changes through sunshine and rain.

Where the preached gospel goes forward accompanied by the Spirit, God's paths overflow with abundance.

The gospel will reach the wilderness and the nations. People will hear, rejoice and bear fruits of righteousness through Jesus Christ, to the Father's glory.

Lord, your works of creation and grace are many and marvelous. In loving-kindness you made them all.
classic_reading:
[Ps.65.1-Ps.65.5]
Chapter 65
Chapter Outline
God is to be praised in the kingdom of grace. | (1-5) |
In the kingdom of providence. | (6-13) |
Verses 1-5
All the praise the Lord receives from this earth is from Zion, being the fruit of the Spirit of Christ, and acceptable through him. Praise is silent unto thee, as wanting words to express the great goodness of God. He reveals himself upon a mercy-seat, ready to hear and answer the prayers of all who come unto him by faith in Jesus Christ. Our sins prevail against us; we cannot pretend to balance them with any righteousness of our own: yet, as for our transgressions, of thine own free mercy, and for the sake of a righteousness of thine own providing, we shall not come into condemnation for them. Observe what it is to come into communion with God in order to blessedness. It is to converse with him as one we love and value; it is to apply ourselves closely to religion as to the business of our dwelling-place. Observe how we come into communion with God; only by God's free choice. There is abundance of goodness in God's house, and what is satisfying to the soul; there is enough for all, enough for each: it is always ready; and all without money and without price. By faith and prayer we may keep up communion with God, and bring in comfort from him, wherever we are. But it is only through that blessed One, who approaches the Father as our Advocate and Surety, that sinners may expect or can find this happiness.
[Ps.65.6-Ps.65.13]
Verses 6-13
That Almighty strength which sets fast the mountains, upholds the believer. That word which stills the stormy ocean, and speaks it into a calm, can silence our enemies. How contrary soever light and darkness are to each other, it is hard to say which is most welcome. Does the watchman wait for the morning? so does the labourer earnestly desire the shades of evening. Some understand it of the morning and evening sacrifices. We are to look upon daily worship, both alone and with our families, to be the most needful of our daily occupations, the most delightful of our daily comforts. How much the fruitfulness of this lower part of the creation depends upon the influence of the upper, is easy to observe; every good and perfect gift is from above. He who enriches the earth, which is filled with man's sins, by his abundant and varied bounty, can neither want power nor will to feed the souls of his people. Temporal mercies to us unworthy creatures, shadow forth more important blessings. The rising of the Sun of righteousness, and the pouring forth of the influences of the Holy Spirit, that river of God, full of the waters of life and salvation, render the hard, barren, worthless hearts of sinners fruitful in every good work, and change the face of nations more than the sun and rain change the face of nature. Wherever the Lord passes, by his preached gospel, attended by his Holy Spirit, his paths drop fatness, and numbers are taught to rejoice in and praise him. They will descend upon the pastures of the wilderness, all the earth shall hear and embrace the gospel, and bring forth abundantly the fruits of righteousness which are, through Jesus Christ, to the glory of the Father. Manifold and marvellous, O Lord, are thy works, whether of nature or of grace; surely in loving-kindness hast thou made them all.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesPraise for God's sovereign power in the creation.1–7For his favour to his church.8–12And the psalmist's praise for his experience of God's goodness.13–20
Praise for God's sovereign power (verses 1–7)

The holy church throughout the world should raise its voice to praise the name above every name.

By both words and deeds, believers should make the praise of Jesus glorious, so that others will be moved to glorify him.

No one can praise God rightly unless his effective grace recreates the heart in holiness.

The redemption accomplished through Christ's death and the wonderful deliverances that flow from it are greater works than Israel's rescue from Egyptian slavery.

We should remember these mighty acts when inviting all the nations to worship God.

God's kindness toward his church (verses 8–12)

The Lord not only preserves our bodily lives; he sustains the spiritual life he has given believers.

Through suffering, his people are tested like silver in the furnace.

The trials of the church will certainly end well.

Through conflicts and troubles, people enslaved by Satan are delivered from his rule and brought to joy and peace in believing.

Believers must pass through many tribulations before entering God's kingdom.

A testimony to answered prayer (verses 13–20)

Tell others who fear God what he has done for your soul.

Describe how he heard and answered prayer, and invite them to join in thanksgiving. This encourages everyone and brings glory to the Lord.

But the comforts of fellowship with God cannot be enjoyed while we cherish the love of sin in the heart, even if we avoid openly committing it.

Deliberately protecting a cherished sin destroys the comfort and effectiveness of prayer. God finds the sacrifice of the wicked detestable.

There is, however, an important difference between welcoming sinful desires and grieving over their presence while firmly resisting them.

If we feel sin within but sincerely long to be freed from it and refuse its demands, that is evidence of genuine repentance and sincerity.

Prayers offered with simplicity and godly sincerity will be answered according to God's goodness.

Then our gratitude rises toward the One who has not turned away either our prayer or his mercy.

Prayer did not obtain deliverance by its own power; God's mercy sent the deliverance.

That mercy is the foundation of hope, the fountain of comfort and the proper object of praise.

For his favour to his church. | (8-12) |

Verses 1-7
The holy church throughout all the world lifts up her voice, to laud that Name which is above every name, to make the praise of Jesus glorious, both by word and deed; that others may be led to glorify him also. But nothing can bring men to do this aright, unless his effectual grace create their hearts anew unto holiness; and in the redemption by the death of Christ, and the glorious deliverances it effects, are more wondrous works than Israel's deliverance from Egyptian bondage.
[Ps.66.8-Ps.66.12]
Verses 8-12
The Lord not only preserves our temporal life, but maintains the spiritual life which he has given to believers. By afflictions we are proved, as silver in the fire. The troubles of the church will certainly end well. Through various conflicts and troubles, the slave of Satan escapes from his yoke, and obtains joy and peace in believing: through much tribulation the believer must enter into the kingdom of God.
[Ps.66.13-Ps.66.20]
Verses 13-20
We should declare unto those that fear God, what he has done for our souls, and how he has heard and answered our prayers, inviting them to join us in prayer and praise; this will turn to our mutual comfort, and to the glory of God. We cannot share these spiritual privileges, if we retain the love of sin in our hearts, though we refrain from the gross practice, Sin, regarded in the heart, will spoil the comfort and success of prayer; for the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination of the Lord. But if the feeling of sin in the heart causes desires to be rid of it; if it be the presence of one urging a demand we know we must not, cannot comply with, this is an argument of sincerity. And when we pray in simplicity and godly sincerity, our prayers will be answered. This will excite gratitude to Him who hath not turned away our prayer nor his mercy from us. It was not prayer that fetched the deliverance, but his mercy that sent it. That is the foundation of our hopes, the fountain of our comforts; and ought to be the matter of our praises.

modern_osis:
Original heading

A prayer for the enlargement of Christ's kingdom.

A prayer for the nations

Every part of our happiness depends upon God's mercy. Therefore the first request is that God show mercy to sinners like us and forgive our sins.

Forgiveness comes through his blessing and is secured in it.

If we walk with him through faith, we may hope for his face to shine upon us.

The psalmist then prayed for the conversion of the Gentiles.

This shows that the saints of the Old Testament desired the privileges they enjoyed to be shared with others.

Many biblical promises and prophecies appear in the form of prayers.

God's answers to the prayers of the church are as certain as the fulfillment of his promises.

The joy desired for the nations is holy joy.

Let them rejoice that the Lord governs kingdoms by Providence and will bring even the kingdoms of this world under the reign of Christ.

That prospect offers every blessing.

The spread of the gospel brings benefits even to earthly society: righteousness exalts a nation.

God's blessing makes our created comforts genuinely sweet and useful.

The psalm looks forward to the whole world worshiping the Lord.

Once the gospel begins to spread, it continues onward until it reaches the ends of the earth.

It is good to join those whom God blesses.

Without Scripture's promises about the conversion of nations, efforts to evangelize them might appear hopeless.

But God has spoken so confidently that we may undertake missionary work trusting he will fulfill his word.

How could we refuse to share the knowledge of God and the salvation in which we rejoice?

Those who have never heard cannot learn unless someone teaches them.

Let us therefore go forward in God's strength and seek the Holy Spirit's accompanying power upon the proclaimed word.

Then Satan's kingdom will be overthrown, and our Redeemer's kingdom established.
classic_reading:
[Ps.67.1]
Chapter 67
A prayer for the enlargement of Christ's kingdom.
--All our happiness comes from God's mercy; therefore the first thing prayed for is, God be merciful to us, to us sinners, and pardon our sins. Pardon is conveyed by God's blessing, and secured in that. If we, by faith, walk with God, we may hope that his face will shine on us. The psalmist passes on to a prayer for the conversion of the Gentiles, which shows that the Old Testament saints desired that their advantages might also be enjoyed by others. And many Scripture prophecies and promises are wrapped up in prayers: the answer to the prayer of the church is as sure as the performance of God's promises. The joy wished to the nations, is holy joy. Let them be glad that by his providence the Lord will overrule the affairs of kingdoms; that even the kingdoms of this world shall became the kingdom of the Lord, and of his Christ. Then is declared a joyful prospect of all good when God shall do this. The success of the gospel brings outward mercies with it; righteousness exalts a nation. The blessing of the Lord sweetens all our creature-comforts to us, and makes them comforts indeed. All the world shall be brought to worship Him. When the gospel begins to spread, it shall go forward more and more, till it reaches to the ends of the earth. It is good to cast in our lot with those that are the blessed of the Lord. If nothing had been spoken in Scripture respecting the conversion of the heathen, we might think it vain to attempt so hopeless a work. But when we see with what confidence it is declared in the Scriptures, we may engage in missionary labours, assured that God will fulfil his own word. And shall we be backward to make known to the heathen the knowledge with which we are favoured, and the salvation we profess to glory in? They cannot learn unless they are taught. Then let us go forward in the strength of the Lord, and look to him to accompany the word the Holy Ghost; then Satan's kingdom shall be destroyed, and the kingdom of our Redeemer established.

God's greatness and tender compassion (verses 1–6)

No one has hardened the heart against God and found lasting prosperity.

The Lord is his people's joy. Let them rejoice when they come before him.

God receives his existence from no one; he is the source of every created being.

Yet he has freely committed himself through promise and covenant to bless his people.

We should praise him for mercy and compassion.

He continually cares for the afflicted and oppressed.

Repenting sinners are helpless and exposed, even more so than fatherless children. God receives them into his own family and makes them sharers in its blessings.

God's remarkable care for Israel (verses 7–14)

Fresh experiences of mercy should awaken memories of earlier mercies.

When God leads his people into a wilderness, he goes before them there and will also lead them out.

He sustained Israel in the wilderness and later in Canaan. The daily manna seems especially relevant to this passage.

These provisions also picture the nourishment of God's spiritual Israel.

The Spirit of grace and the gospel of grace are the generous rain that strengthens the Lord's inheritance and makes it fruitful.

Christ comes like showers watering the earth.

The record of Israel's victories looks forward to the exalted Redeemer's triumph over death and hell for all who belong to him.

Israel's suffering in Egypt's brick kilns seemed wretched.

Its later glory in Canaan under David and Solomon seemed wonderful by contrast.

So those once enslaved by Satan become honorable when justified and sanctified through Christ.

When they enter heaven, the last remnants of sin disappear.

They become like the wings of a dove covered in silver and its feathers shining gold.

Through complete salvation, those once filthy with guilt become white as snow.

The ascended Christ bestows gifts (verses 15–21)

Henry understands these verses as speaking especially of Christ's ascension, as Paul applies them in Ephesians 4:8.

Through the purchase of his death, Christ received the gifts necessary for sinners' conversion and believers' salvation.

He continually distributes these gifts, even among people formerly rebellious, so that the Lord may live among them as Friend and Father.

As Jesus said, the Father gave him authority over all people to give eternal life to those entrusted to him (John 17:2).

Christ came to a rebellious world not to condemn it, but that the world might be saved through him.

He is Savior and Benefactor to his willing people, but a consuming fire to those who persist in rebellion.

His gifts are so many and weighty that God can be said to load us with benefits.

He will not offer merely temporary comforts as our inheritance: he himself will be the God of our salvation.

Christ removes death's sting for believers when they die and grants complete victory over death when they rise again.

He will strike down the pride of the enemy and crush the serpent's head.

Christ's victories for his people (verses 22–28)

The victories God gave David over Israel's enemies pictured Christ's victories for himself and everyone trusting him.

Those who take him as their Savior can regard him as their God and King acting for their good, answering their prayers, especially through his word and appointed ordinances.

The Messiah's kingdom will gain the submission of rulers and learned people across the world.

Henry notes that verse 28 seems to address the king.

Yet its words may be applied to the Redeemer, his church and every sincere believer.

We pray: Lord Jesus, complete the undertaking you began for us by finishing your good work within us.

The nations invited into the church (verses 29–31)

The psalm gives an urgent invitation to those still outside God's church.

Some submit because fear and conscience compel them, as Providence exposes the foolishness of their opposition and draws them to make peace with the church.

Others submit willingly.

Henry associates both responses with the language of verses 29 and 31.

The beauty and goodness of serving God, and of the gospel that went out from Jerusalem, are sufficient reasons to invite sinners from every nation.

All power belongs to God (verses 32–35)

All who worship in God's holy places should admire and adore him with reverence and godly fear.

The God of Israel gives his people strength and power.

Only through Christ strengthening us can we do what he calls us to do.

We must therefore give him every part of the glory, thanking him humbly for enabling our work and for graciously accepting what his own hands accomplish within us.

[Ps.68.1-Ps.68.6]
Chapter 68
Chapter Outline
A prayer--The greatness and goodness of God.
(1-6)
The wonderful works God wrought for his people. | (7-14) |
The presence of God in his church. | (15-21) |
The victories of Christ. | (22-28) |
Enlargement of the church. | (29-31) |
The glory and grace of God. | (32-35) |
Verses 1-6
None ever hardened his heart against God, and prospered. God is the joy of his people, then let them rejoice when they come before him. He who derives his being from none, but gives being to all, is engaged by promise and covenant to bless his people. He is to be praised as a God of mercy and tender compassion. He ever careth for the afflicted and oppressed: repenting sinners, who are helpless and exposed more than any fatherless children, are admitted into his family, and share all their blessings.
[Ps.68.7-Ps.68.14]
Verses 7-14
Fresh mercies should put us in mind of former mercies. If God bring his people into a wilderness, he will be sure to go before them in it, and to bring them out of it. He provided for them, both in the wilderness and in Canaan. The daily manna seems here meant. And it looks to the spiritual provision for God's Israel. The Spirit of grace and the gospel of grace are the plentiful rain, with which God confirms his inheritance, and from which their fruit is found. Christ shall come as showers that water the earth. The account of Israel's victories is to be applied to the victories over death and hell, by the exalted Redeemer, for those that are his. Israel in Egypt among the kilns appeared wretched, but possessed of Canaan, during the reigns of David and Solomon, appeared glorious. Thus the slaves of Satan, when converted to Christ, when justified and sanctified by him, look honourable. When they reach heaven, all remains of their sinful state disappear, they shall be as the wings of the dove, covered with silver, and her feathers as gold. Full salvation will render those white as snow, who were vile and loathsome through the guilt and defilement of sin.
[Ps.68.15-Ps.68.21]
Verses 15-21
The ascension of Christ must here be meant, and thereto it is applied, [Eph.4.8] Ep 4:8. He received as the purchase of his death, the gifts needful for the conversion of sinners, and the salvation of believers. These he continually bestows, even on rebellious men, that the Lord God might dwell among them, as their Friend and Father. He gave gifts to men. Having received power to give eternal life, the Lord Jesus bestows it on as many as were given him, [John.17.2] Joh 17:2. Christ came to a rebellious world, not to condemn it, but that through him it might be saved. The glory of Zion's King is, that he is a Saviour and Benefactor to all his willing people, and a consuming fire to all that persist in rebellion against him. So many, so weighty are the gifts of God's bounty, that he may be truly said to load us with them. He will not put us off with present things for a portion, but will be the God of our salvation. The Lord Jesus has authority and power to rescue his people from the dominion of death, by taking away the sting of it from them when they die, and giving them complete victory over it when they rise again. The crown of the head, the chief pride and glory of the enemy, shall be smitten; Christ shall crush the head of the serpent.
[Ps.68.22-Ps.68.28]
Verses 22-28
The victories with which God blessed David over the enemies of Israel, are types of Christ's victory, for himself and for all believers. Those who take him for theirs, may see him acting as their God, as their King, for their good, and in answer to their prayers; especially in and by his word and ordinances. The kingdom of the Messiah shall be submitted to by all the rulers and learned in the world. The people seem to address the king, ver. #(28). But the words are applicable to the Redeemer, to his church, and every true believer. We pray, that thou, O God the Son, wilt complete thine undertaking for us, by finishing thy good work in us.
[Ps.68.29-Ps.68.31]
Verses 29-31
A powerful invitation is given to those that are without, to join the church. Some shall submit from fear; overcome by their consciences, and the checks of Providence, they are brought to make peace with the church. Others will submit willingly, ver. #(29-31). There is that beauty and benefit in the service of God, and in the gospel of Christ which went forth from Jerusalem, which is enough to invite sinners out of all nations.
[Ps.68.32-Ps.68.35]
Verses 32-35
God is to be admired and adored with reverence and godly fear, by all that attend in his holy places. The God of Israel gives strength and power unto his people. Through Christ strengthening us we can do all things, not otherwise; therefore he must have the glory of all we do, with our humble thanks for enabling us to do it, and for accepting the work of his hands in us.

The sufferings of David and Christ (verses 1–12)

We should regularly contemplate the Person who suffered in this psalm, and ask not merely what he suffered but why.

Meditation on Christ's suffering should humble us for our sins, awaken us to their danger and fill us with gratitude and love that move us to live for the One who died to save us.

When afflicted, entrust the soul to God. This keeps suffering from making us bitter or driving us toward despair.

David was wrongfully hated, but these words apply more fully to Jesus Christ.

Because injustice is common, we should not be surprised when people become our enemies without cause.

Our concern should be that we never do wrong ourselves. Then we can better bear wrong committed against us.

Through his blood Christ made satisfaction for our sins, restoring what he had not taken away and paying a debt that was ours.

Even when innocent of human accusations, we must acknowledge that before God our own sins deserve judgment.

Our sins spring from folly and are all committed in the Lord's sight.

David suffered rejection from friends and family.

Christ also faced unbelief from his brothers and desertion by his disciples.

He made satisfaction not only through the honors he rendered to God, but also by submitting to extraordinary public dishonor.

If zeal for God's truth, commandments or worship brings mockery, we should not lose courage.

Prayer when trouble overwhelms us (verses 13–21)

Whatever deep waters of affliction, temptation or oppression seem to engulf us, we should persevere in prayer for the Lord's salvation.

Even in severe outward trouble, signs of God's favor can keep the soul from sinking.

If we continue thinking rightly of God during hardships, we can trust him to deal wisely and kindly with us.

When we suffer reproach for Christ's name, it comforts us that he knows our shame.

A damaged reputation pains someone who values a good name.

Yet being considered worthy to suffer for Jesus should prevent that pain from overwhelming us.

The psalm foretold aspects of Christ's suffering so accurately that its fulfillment confirms Scripture's divine truth and Jesus as the true Messiah.

The vinegar and gall given to him were a faint image of the far more bitter cup he drank so that we could receive the cup of salvation.

We should expect little from human comforters and much from the God of all consolation.

Divine judgment and the offer of mercy (verses 22–29)

Henry understands these words as prophecies of judgment upon Christ's persecutors, not as an instruction for private revenge.

Verses 22 and 23 are applied by Paul to judgment on unbelieving Jews in Romans 11:9–10.

When bodily pleasures and ordinary supports of life become the food and fuel of sin, even the table becomes a snare.

Those people refused to see the light because they loved darkness.

Their punishment was that they could no longer see clearly: God left them to the desires and hardening of their own hearts.

Everyone who rejects the great salvation freely offered by God must take seriously the warning of divine judgment.

Yet even those who have greatly multiplied their sins may still find mercy through the Mediator's righteousness.

God excludes no one from that righteousness who does not, through unbelief, exclude themselves.

Those too proud or stubborn to accept it choose their own ruin.

A person poor and sorrowful with God's blessing is better off than someone rich and cheerful while under his judgment.

Henry also applies this contrast to Christ.

When he lived on earth, he was a Man of Sorrows with nowhere to rest his head. Yet God exalted him.

Let guilty and afflicted sinners call upon God: his salvation lifts them up.

Joy, praise and the future of Zion (verses 30–36)

The psalm began with sorrow and complaint but ends in holy praise.

Humble thanksgiving pleases God more than the most impressive and expensive outward sacrifice.

The humble will seek him and rejoice; those who seek him through Christ will live and receive consolation.

God will accomplish great things for his gospel church.

Let everyone who loves his people rejoice in that prospect.

Future generations will serve him on earth, and his servants will inherit his heavenly kingdom.

Those who love his name will dwell before him forever.

God did not spare his own Son but gave him for us all. With him he will freely give us everything needed for salvation.

Lord, great Restorer of ruined places, arise and turn ungodliness away from your people.

[Ps.69.1-Ps.69.12]
Chapter 69
Chapter Outline
David complains of great distress. | (1-12) |
And begs for succour. | (13-21) |
He declares the judgments of God. | (22-29) |
He concludes with joy and praise. | (30-36) |
Verses 1-12
We should frequently consider the person of the Sufferer here spoken of, and ask why, as well as what he suffered, that, meditating thereon, we may be more humbled for sin, and more convinced of our danger, so that we may feel more gratitude and love, constraining us to live to His glory who died for our salvation. Hence we learn, when in affliction, to commit the keeping of our souls to God, that we may not be soured with discontent, or sink into despair. David was hated wrongfully, but the words far more fully apply to Christ. In a world where unrighteousness reigns so much, we must not wonder if we meet with those that are our enemies wrongfully. Let us take care that we never do wrong; then if we receive wrong, we may the better bear it. By the satisfaction Christ made to God for our sin by his blood, he restored that which he took not away, he paid our debt, suffered for our offences. Even when we can plead Not guilty, as to men's unjust accusations, yet before God we must acknowledge ourselves to deserve all that is brought upon us. All our sins take rise from our foolishness. They are all done in God's sight. David complains of the unkindness of friends and relations. This was fulfilled in Christ, whose brethren did not believe on him, and who was forsaken by his disciples. Christ made satisfaction for us, not only by putting off the honours due to God, but by submitting to the greatest dishonours that could be done to any man. We need not be discouraged if our zeal for the truths, precepts, and worship of God, should provoke some, and cause others to mock our godly sorrow and deadness to the world.
[Ps.69.13-Ps.69.21]
Verses 13-21
Whatever deep waters of affliction or temptation we sink into, whatever floods of trouble or ungodly men seem ready to overwhelm us, let us persevere in prayer to our Lord to save us. The tokens of God's favour to us are enough to keep our spirits from sinking in the deepest outward troubles. If we think well of God, and continue to do so under the greatest hardships, we need not fear but he will do well for us. And if at any time we are called on to suffer reproach and shame, for Christ's sake, this may be our comfort, that he knows it. It bears hard on one that knows the worth of a good name, to be oppressed with a bad one; but when we consider what a favour it is to be accounted worthy to suffer shame for the name of Jesus, we shall see that there is no reason why it should be heart-breaking to us. The sufferings of Christ were here particularly foretold, which proves the Scripture to be the word of God; and how exactly these predictions were fulfilled in Jesus Christ, which proves him to be the true Messiah. The vinegar and the gall given to him, were a faint emblem of that bitter cup which he drank up, that we might drink the cup of salvation. We cannot expect too little from men, miserable comforters are they all; nor can we expect too much from the God of all comfort and consolation.
[Ps.69.22-Ps.69.29]
Verses 22-29
These are prophecies of the destruction of Christ's persecutors. Verses #(22-23), are applied to the judgments of God upon the unbelieving Jews, in [Rom.11.9] Ro 11:9, [Rom.11.10] 10. When the supports of life and delights of sense, through the corruption of our nature, are made the food and fuel of sin, then our table is a snare. Their sin was, that they would not see, but shut their eyes against the light, loving darkness rather; their punishment was, that they should not see, but should be given up to their own hearts' lusts which hardened them. Those who reject God's great salvation proffered to them, may justly fear that his indignation will be poured out upon them. If men will sin, the Lord will reckon for it. But those that have multiplied to sin, may yet find mercy, through the righteousness of the Mediator. God shuts not out any from that righteousness; the gospel excludes none who do not, by unbelief, shut themselves out. But those who are proud and self-willed, so that they will not come in to God's righteousness, shall have their doom accordingly; they themselves decide it. Let those not expect any benefit thereby, who are not glad to be beholden to it. It is better to be poor and sorrowful, with the blessing of the Lord, than rich and jovial, and under his curse. This may be applied to Christ. He was, when on earth, a man of sorrows that had not where to lay his head; but God exalted him. Let us call upon the Lord, and though poor and sorrowful, guilty and defiled, his salvation will set us up on high.
[Ps.69.30-Ps.69.36]
Verses 30-36
The psalmist concludes the psalm with holy joy and praise, which he began with complaints of his grief. It is a great comfort to us, that humble and thankful praises are more pleasing to God than the most costly, pompous sacrifices. The humble shall look to him, and be glad; those that seek him through Christ shall live and be comforted. God will do great things for the gospel church, in which let all who wish well to it rejoice. A seed shall serve him on earth, and his servants shall inherit his heavenly kingdom. Those that love his name shall dwell before him for ever. He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? Arise, thou great Restorer of the ancient places to dwell in, and turn away ungodliness from thy people.

Original heading

The speedy destruction of the wicked, and the preservation of the godly.

Prayer in urgent trouble

This psalm repeats almost the same words as the last five verses of Psalm 40.

Here we see Jesus Christ portrayed in poverty and distress.

At the same time the words announce righteous and fearsome judgment on his enemies—Jewish, pagan and antichristian opponents in Henry's historical and theological language.

The psalm also appeals for the joy and happiness of Christ's friends, to the honor of his Father.

Let us apply its teaching to our own troubles, remembering them and their sinful causes with faith rather than carelessness or resentment.

Urgent trials should awaken earnest prayer.

Chapter 70
The speedy destruction of the wicked, and the preservation of the godly.
--This psalm is almost the same as the last five verses of Psa 40. While here we behold Jesus Christ set forth in poverty and distress, we also see him denouncing just and fearful punishment on his Jewish, heathen, and antichristian enemies; and pleading for the joy and happiness of his friends, to his Father's honour. Let us apply these things to our own troubled circumstances, and in a believing manner bring them, and the sinful causes thereof, to our remembrance. Urgent trials should always awake fervent prayers.
